title: TypeScript compiler ported to C# via Codex (as proof of concept)
content:
Warning
This project was created as a case study and will not be actively maintained. It is provided as-is; ongoing fixes, updates, and support are not planned.
A C# port of the pinned Go TypeScript compiler, with project checking, ordinary Program emit and a real language server. The agreed compiler and language-services contracts are complete and independently verified under Linux x64 Native AOT. This is a pinned-upstream implementation, not a claim of complete repository, all-platform or every historical TypeScript feature parity.
Performance on vscode project:
The reference is Microsoft TypeScript revision
fed0bf24149fb1ed36039212648bafdafc1ea10e.
See the upstream record, current state,
compiler assessment and
language-services assessment.
I know, "another port 🙄".
But the lazy Rust port from last week struck close to home. I'm a bit of a TypeScript geek and I learned Golang way back during Stripe CTF3; a performance context and even clenching a 4th place in the document indexing round. Which some may remember was scaffolded in Scala.. Well I noped the f out of that and wrote it in Go 😂. And I'm a C# Stan.
So this Rust port claimed to burn up "400k in ChatGPT!!!" and Codex couldn't get the job done after months. Opus 5.5 to the rescue in 10 hours and you could do it for "$20k!!".
Wut?! Hold my 🍺
- Use Codex
- Port TypeScript from Golang to C#
- Adhere closely to the Golang source
- Optimize it to within +20% of Golang projects performance on VSCODE
- Do it cheap!
- Learn some shit
Way back it was curious to me the TypeScript team selected Golang instead of C#. IIRC DotNet native AOT was still early days and Golang had more portability.. Also a lot of judgement calls over the suitability and how closely the concepts mapped; all understandable in the era of hand-porting code LOL. But I always wondered how fast a C# implementation could be..
That last bit.. I wanted to see if the process could be optimized through early high-level strategy and steering where necessary.
Not to bury the lede => Cost was ~$75-100 USD
The basic setup was an Astra project coordinator delegating coding, research, and review tasks to 6.1 Sol sub agents.
I worked with ChatpGPT(Astra) to produce the prompt provided to the agent. I explained my desire to stick close to the Golang source and to execute the work as efficiently as possible.
The prompt was then provided to Codex.
As it got going I suggested it record a re-entry in case the session was lost or the VM crashed(which it did!). And provided a few more steering ideas as I observed the work. I installed Sqlite for it to use for coordination, but it opted to stick with files throughout TMK.
At this stage it was executing bounded vertical slices because I phrased the project as a "feasibility study". After it finished a campaign(what it started calling sprints?) I would take the summary back to ChatGPT and we'd decide the next chunk of work and a new prompt fed in to continue..
After a few rounds I determined the token burn was low enough to finish the entire port cheaply, and moved to have the entire checker completed. The agent continued to expand the outer implementation boundary one "bounded vertical slice" at a time though.. This proving hugely inefficient as it kept running into hacks and kludges it contructed to make the feature slices "work" without error 🙃
This was leading to tons of "churn" through test/analyze/fix cycles every time a missing bit of functionlity was hit. I directed it to start completing entire subsystem dependencies comprehensively and this made a big improvement.
At this point I also noticed the agent had created tons of internal state partiy tests. It put code into the Golang project to record states of caches and etc and.. It became fixated on differences that seemed like they would have no externally observable impact, or that the upstream test suite should catch eventually anyway..
So I directed it away from doing that which seemed to really accelerate work.
At this point it was give the "epic" of completing checker parity. A new efficiency issue popped up where after subagents checked in fixes for tests it would run the entire fracking regression suite it built. I steered it towards targetted testing and deferring full regression for end of epic and this proved super helpful.
From here on much less steering occured. Checker was finished and validated against the VSCODE project. And then we started the major performance push. Golang was allocating ~5.1G during the vscode project type check and we were doing like ~56G!!! Wall time was 6x+ 😭
Here is the summary of the work that got us within +20% Golang: PERF EPIC SUMMARY
After checker the Emit and LSP epics were fed in and laregely required no stearing. The recorded perf epic lessons were used to get vscode complilation with emit to within +8.5% golang with no extre input from me..
The LSP epic took about 12 hours, completely unattended.
How work is carried out plays a huge role in the outcome; both the quality of results and how much token spend it took to get there. Some high-level strategy and a few process stearing can go a long way.
Hats off to the TypeScript team.. A lot has to do with idiomatic Golang being quite efficient in memory allocation and sharing compared to idtiomatic C#. But it's quite thoroughly adhered to and absolutely mopped the floor with the LLMs first checker parity build.
Agents can get fixated on a few tasks and start ignoring other responsibilities. The coordinator agent had a lot on its plate including being responsible for efficient execution of the project. However it was sometimes blind to obvious(to me) inefficiencies in the process that crept in.
I believe a layer above the coordinator focused on analyzing and steering the coordinator on process efficiency could have potentially replaced me taking that role.
- Checks configured, multi-file projects using genuine compiler options, module resolution, project references and standard libraries.
- Emits JavaScript, declarations and source maps through the ported upstream transformations, printer and output infrastructure.
- Maintains editor projects, snapshots, overlays, unsaved/incremental document changes, parse/config caches, checker leases, autoimports and file watches.
- Serves diagnostics, completion/resolve, hover, signature help, definitions, references, implementations, rename, symbols, formatting, organize imports, registered code actions, semantic tokens, inlay hints, selection/folding ranges, call hierarchy and code lenses through the upstream LSP surface.
- Handles real stdio framing, negotiated positions and capabilities, cancellation, client requests, progress, registration, shutdown, signals and parent monitoring.
All 115 pinned standard-library declaration files are embedded unchanged. The library and CLI target .NET 10; global.json pins the build SDK.
From the repository root, use .NET SDK 10.0.401 selected by global.json
and the Linux Native AOT native compiler/zlib development prerequisites (on Ubuntu,
clang and zlib1g-dev):
dotnet publish src/TypeScript.Check/TypeScript.Check.csproj \
  -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true -p:StripSymbols=true \
  -o artifacts/tscheck
Compile a genuine TypeScript configuration, or check without writing outputs:
artifacts/tscheck/tscheck --config path/to/tsconfig.json --json
artifacts/tscheck/tscheck --config path/to/tsconfig.json --noEmit --json
artifacts/tscheck/tscheck --config path/to/tsconfig.json --listFilesOnly
Compiler options determine JavaScript, declaration and map outputs. Success exits
0; compiler errors exit 1 when emit is skipped and 2 otherwise. --listFilesOnly
is a command flag, not a tsconfig option. Existing --project <tscheck.json> retains
its check-only compatibility behavior. Configuration and graph inspection are
available through --inspect-config, --inspect-project and --inspect-program.
See the configuration, resolution
and Program guides.
Start the public language server:

report.summary: A developer used OpenAI Codex agents to port the Go-based TypeScript compiler to C#, reaching within 20% of Go's performance for roughly $100.
report.background: Microsoft's native TypeScript compiler was written in Go rather than C#, a decision made when .NET Native AOT was immature and Go offered stronger portability and conceptual fit for a hand-ported codebase. The author, a long-time C# and TypeScript enthusiast, always wondered how fast an idiomatic C# implementation could be — especially now that .NET 10 AOT is production-ready. The project was also a direct response to a recent LLM-driven Rust port, whose reported costs and timelines were used as a benchmark. The wider context is that agentic coding tools like Codex are making large, cross-language codebase ports newly feasible, shifting the hard problems from typing code to steering the process, verifying correctness, and containing token spend.
key_points: The port cost roughly $75–100 in tokens, far below the six-figure figures cited for a comparable Rust effort. Work was coordinated by an 'Astra' planner delegating coding, research and review to Codex sub-agents, with the human supplying prompt framing and periodic process steering.

Performance was the hard part. The first checker-parity build allocated around 56 GB during the VS Code project type-check versus Go's ~5.1 GB, with wall time over 6x slower. A dedicated performance epic closed that gap to within +20% of Go, and emit later landed within +8.5%.

Feature coverage is broad: real tsconfig handling, module resolution, project references, JavaScript/declaration/source-map emit, plus a working LSP server with completion, hover, rename, references, semantic tokens, inlay hints and code actions. All 115 pinned standard-library declaration files are embedded unchanged.

Much of the learning was about process, not code. Bounded vertical slices encouraged kludges and constant churn, so the agent was redirected to complete whole subsystems. It also over-ran full regression suites after every fix and fixated on internal state-parity tests with no observable effect.

The project is explicitly a pinned-upstream feasibility study, not maintained and not a claim of all-platform or complete historical TypeScript parity. It targets .NET 10 on Linux x64 Native AOT and the public language server can be launched directly.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is another data point that agentic coding can execute large, multi-month engineering projects for double-digit dollars, which puts pressure on how companies scope and price porting and migration work. For developers, it weakens the assumption that only one language is viable for a high-performance compiler: C# with modern Native AOT can be competitive with idiomatic Go, and the repository doubles as a reference implementation and benchmark. For regular users, nothing changes in the short term — this is a proof of concept, not a shipping toolchain. The more durable lesson is that steering, subsystem-level planning and targeted testing, not raw model capability, dominate both quality and cost.
report.tools: Follow microsoft/typescript-go (the official native port) for upstream ground truth, and stepwisehq/typescript-dotnet for this C# case study and its compiler/LSP assessments. To experiment, install the .NET 10 SDK with Native AOT prerequisites and publish the check project for linux-x64. Also worth watching: OpenAI Codex and similar agent orchestrators, the TypeScript language-server protocol for tooling work, and Roslyn/VS Code extension samples if you want to wire the emitted LSP into an editor.
